content: The desirable and undesirable effects of the recommendation, the overall quality of the evidence, the values and preferences associated with the recommendation in various settings, and the cost implications for public health authorities in implementing the recommendation were all carefully considered. These factors were discussed among the members of the WHO Nutrition Guidance Expert Advisory Group (NUGAG), invited external experts, and the WHO Secretariat present at the meeting. The final wording of the recommendations and their strength were determined based on a consensus among the NUGAG members and the WHO Secretariat. There were no significant disagreements among the NUGAG members. From February 1 to February 29, 2012, a draft of the guideline was made available for public comment. Members of the External Expert and Stakeholder Panel were consulted, and other interested parties were invited to provide feedback. Over 165 comments were received from 30 individuals and representatives of stakeholder groups. WHO reviewed these comments and made appropriate updates to the guideline. The finalized guideline was presented to the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health during their meeting from March 27 to March 30, 2012, for finalization. The finalized guideline was then submitted for clearance by WHO before publication. In accordance with WHO's rules, all experts participating in WHO meetings were required to declare any relevant interests before participating. The declaration of interest forms for all guideline group members were reviewed by WHO when finalizing the composition of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health. All NUGAG members, external experts, and special invitees participating in the meetings submitted a declaration of interests form along with their curriculum vitae. Additionally, each participant verbally declared their interests at the beginning of each meeting. The management of interests strictly adhered to WHO's guidelines for the declaration of interests for experts. A summary of the potential interests declared by members of the NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health, as well as external experts and resource persons, is provided in Annex 9. This guideline is based on a comprehensive review of epidemiological literature, including three new systematic reviews conducted by WHO to summarize the evidence regarding potassium intake and health outcomes. Specific health outcomes considered in adults included blood pressure, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, stroke, coronary heart disease, renal function, blood lipids, catecholamine levels, and other potential adverse effects. In children, the outcomes considered were blood pressure, blood lipids, catecholamine levels, and other potential adverse effects. The systematic reviews addressed specific research questions, such as the effect of increased potassium intake compared to lower potassium intake on health outcomes in adults and children. The reviews also examined the effects of varying levels of potassium intake (e.g., less than 90 mmol/day, 90–120 mmol/day, 120–155 mmol/day, and more than 155 mmol/day) on health outcomes. Evidence was considered conclusive for either benefit or harm if the point estimate suggested a benefit or harm and the 95% confidence interval (CI) did not overlap a threshold of clinical relevance. If the real value at the high or low 95% CI was not clinically relevant, the evidence was considered conclusive of no effect. In such cases, point estimates were deemed precise or imprecise based on the clinical relevance of the CI values. WHO conducted a systematic review to explore the relationship between potassium intake and blood pressure in adults. The review identified 22 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 17 were conducted in individuals with hypertension (defined as blood pressure ≥140/90 mmHg), three in individuals without hypertension, and two in mixed populations. Two studies included only women, while the remaining 20 included both men and women. The studies were conducted globally and measured 24-hour urinary potassium excretion. The findings demonstrated that increasing potassium intake is beneficial for blood pressure across a wide range of baseline intakes. The greatest impact on blood pressure was observed with potassium intake of approximately 90–120 mmol/day. WHO also conducted a systematic review on the relationship between potassium consumption and cardiovascular disease, stroke, coronary heart disease, and all-cause mortality. The review updated and reanalyzed data from a recent systematic review by D’Elia and colleagues. Twelve prospective cohort studies with over 127,000 participants measured potassium intake through urinary excretion, dietary records, or a combination of methods. These studies compared the incidence of cardiovascular disease, stroke, or coronary heart disease between the lowest and highest potassium-consuming groups. The results suggested a positive effect of increased potassium intake on stroke, further supporting the conclusion that increasing potassium intake has beneficial effects on health. In children, WHO conducted a systematic review of the effect of increased potassium intake on blood pressure, blood lipids, catecholamine levels, and other potential adverse effects. Only four studies in children met the inclusion criteria, and none reported on blood lipids, catecholamine levels, or other adverse effects. Three of the studies were controlled trials conducted in the USA, involving 326 boys and girls with an average age of 13 years. The fourth study was an observational cohort study conducted in the Netherlands, which followed children aged 5–17 years for seven years. The results of the cohort study were consistent with a beneficial effect of increased potassium intake on blood pressure over time. Although there were few high-quality RCTs testing the effect of increased potassium intake on blood pressure and potential adverse effects in children, data from systematic reviews conducted in adults were used to estimate the effect of potassium intake on health outcomes in children. Renal function is fully developed in early childhood, making it acceptable to extrapolate findings from adults to children. The results suggest that an increase in potassium intake, whether from supplements or food, has a beneficial effect on blood pressure. The body efficiently adapts to and excretes excess potassium via urine when consumption exceeds needs, and there have been no reports of potassium toxicity from food consumption. No minor side effects from increased potassium intake were reported in any of the RCTs, and the absence of adverse effects is consistent with the literature. The consistency in results from studies with increased potassium through dietary changes supports the health benefits of potassium specifically, rather than the conjugate anion found in supplements.
